newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria CA bidders silent on tender.
newsitem.headline: Austria CA bidders silent on tender.

text.p: Bidders for Austria's flagship bank Creditanstalt are holding their cards close to their chest after Finance Minister Viktor Klima on Friday reopened the tender to allow existing offers to be improved.

Bank Austria, which has made an offer of 836 schillings per share for the whole of the government's 70 percent stake in Creditanstalt, would say nothing except that it had received a letter from Klima and was analysing it. Its bid amounts to a total of 16.7 billion schillings.
An Austro-Italian consortium led by EA-Generali had not yet made any decision on whether it would raise its offer, spokesman Josef Hlinka told Reuters.
"We have not got as far as making a definite decision. We are analysing the situation," he said.

EA-Generali has offered 730 schillings per share for 14.7 million shares and 580 schillings for the remaining 5.2 million shares, which it plans to float on the stock market, according to the finance ministry.
The third bidder Austrian entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek was not available for comment. His bid is estimated around 15 billion schillings.
The state's holding in Austria's second biggest bank is worth 14.5 billion schillings at market prices.
Klima would not make any comment on the sale, which has been dragging on for six years, but his spokesman David Mock said changes to the composition of the bidding parties were not permitted.
"If anyone is considering taking someone else on, that's not allowed," Mock said on Monday. "Any new partners would be a breach of the legal offer."

The bid by Bank Austria, effectively controlled by Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna, for Creditanstalt which is a conservative stronghold, has set the cat among the pigeons within the government coalition of Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party.

The People's Party on Monday demanded an emergency session of parliament early in the New Year to push through changes to the law on privatisation and floatation to prevent the government selling the bank to "socialist" Bank Austria.
